chapter: Chicago repertoire, bands and the end of the big-band era
title: Regional sounds and the Coltrane clones
summary: Freeman says records erased regional band styles and that Coltrane imitators made Trane himself more popular.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: What about the regional stuff? Did you hear a big difference between like – at that time, it seemed to be more of a bigger difference when bands came from different regions, like a band that came from Kansas City area. It was a huge . . .

Oh yeah, of course. Well, they lost that with the advent of records, everybody listening to the same records. Like when Trane came in, Trane wiped out everybody, because everybody said, “I’ve got to play like Coltrane.” Everybody said, “But man, you’re not going anywhere being a Coltrane clone.” “I don’t care. I got to play this.” So consequently now, how many Tranes is it?

Now there you go. People go to the record store, and they don’t buy those clones, because what they did was, they made Trane more popular. They said, “That sounds good, but where’s the cat that was doing the style on this? Oh, okay.” So they buy Trane. And Trane’s been gone since when? ’67? He’s more popular now than he ever was. The guys are finally realizing that, that they don’t have to try to come past Trane, because they’re not going to do that anyway. So just get whatever you dig about Trane, and then head out.
